title: Pre-Modern Economies
description: From subsistence to civilization to trade

concepts.title: Agriculture & Civilizations
concepts.contentHtml:
The Neolithic agricultural revolution (~10,000 BCE) transformed human economies from hunter-gatherer subsistence to settled farming, surplus production, and population growth.

Surplus enabled non-farming specialists: priests, soldiers, craftsmen, scribes, rulers. Cities, writing, and complex states followed. Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus Valley, China — all developed similar economic and political institutions independently.

For most of subsequent history, agricultural productivity capped how many non-farmers a society could support. ~80-90% of pre-industrial populations were farmers.

concepts.title: Ancient Trade Networks
concepts.contentHtml:
Long-distance trade existed millennia before modern globalization. The Silk Road (~200 BCE-1450 CE) connected China to the Mediterranean, exchanging silk, spices, glass, ideas. Indian Ocean monsoon trade linked East Africa, Arabia, India, Southeast Asia.

The trans-Saharan trade carried gold and salt across the desert. The Hanseatic League dominated Baltic trade in medieval northern Europe. Trade networks were sophisticated, lucrative, and culturally formative.

concepts.title: Money, Credit, Banking
concepts.contentHtml:
Money predates writing — early forms include barley (Mesopotamia), cowrie shells, metals. Coined money emerged in Lydia (~600 BCE) and rapidly spread.

Banking emerged with Italian merchant cities (Medici, Bardi, Peruzzi) in the 13th-15th centuries. Bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping, and joint-stock companies (Dutch and English East India Companies in early 1600s) laid groundwork for modern finance.

Paper money was a Chinese invention (Song dynasty); it spread elsewhere centuries later.

title: Mercantilism & Empire
description: European empires and the rise of capitalism

concepts.title: Age of Mercantilism
concepts.contentHtml:
European powers from ~1500-1800 pursued mercantilism: maximize national wealth through positive trade balances, accumulate gold and silver, protect domestic industries, exploit colonies.

Spain and Portugal extracted vast precious metals from American colonies. Spanish silver from Potosí (Bolivia) and Mexican mines flowed globally — much ended up in China paying for tea, silk, and porcelain.

The Atlantic slave trade and plantation economies (sugar, tobacco, cotton) were crucial to early modern wealth accumulation. Tortuous moral and economic legacies followed.

concepts.title: Joint-Stock Companies
concepts.contentHtml:
The Dutch East India Company (VOC, 1602) and English East India Company (1600) were among the world's first joint-stock corporations — pooling investor capital to fund risky long-distance trade.

VOC was eventually granted quasi-sovereign powers (military, treaties, coinage). It generated enormous wealth and ran what was effectively the world's first multinational corporation.

Joint-stock structure spread financial risk and enabled scale impossible for individual merchants. It's the institutional ancestor of modern public corporations.

concepts.title: Adam Smith and Classical Economics
concepts.contentHtml:
Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) launched modern economics. Smith critiqued mercantilism, argued for free markets, the division of labor, and the 'invisible hand' through which individual self-interest produces collective benefit.

David Ricardo (comparative advantage), Thomas Malthus (population), Karl Marx (labor and capital) followed. Classical economics established frameworks still used today.

The 19th century saw widespread industrialization and the rise of free trade ideology — though always partial in practice.

concepts.title: The Industrial Revolution
concepts.contentHtml:
Beginning in 18th-century Britain, mechanization (steam engines, textile machinery), factory production, and coal-based energy transformed economies. Productivity rose dramatically; new working-class urban populations emerged.

By 1900, Britain, Germany, the US, and parts of France/Belgium were industrial powers. Industrialization spread to Japan (Meiji), Russia, and elsewhere over decades. Industrialization was uneven; major regions (China, India, most of Africa) industrialized late or under colonial constraint.

concepts.title: First Globalization
concepts.contentHtml:
The late 19th century saw a striking globalization: gold standard, falling shipping costs (steamships, telegraphs), mass migration (especially European to Americas), and global capital flows.

Trade as percent of GDP reached levels not seen again until the late 20th century. The world economy became deeply integrated — though under colonial inequality.

WWI and the Great Depression ended this first globalization. Tariffs rose, capital flows reversed, and the world fragmented economically.

concepts.title: The Great Depression
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1929 stock market crash triggered the worst economic downturn in industrial history. US GDP fell ~30%; unemployment reached 25%. Banking collapse, deflation, mass joblessness in industrial countries.

Different responses: the US New Deal (FDR), German Nazi public works and rearmament, British devaluation, Soviet five-year plans (in a separate economic system). Recovery dragged on through the 1930s; full recovery came with WWII rearmament.

The Depression discredited laissez-faire economics in many quarters. Keynesian economics — government should manage demand — became influential. The post-WWII economic order would be substantially shaped by Depression-era lessons.

concepts.title: Bretton Woods System
concepts.contentHtml:
The 1944 Bretton Woods conference designed the postwar monetary order. Currencies pegged to the US dollar; the dollar pegged to gold. The IMF and World Bank were created to stabilize finance and fund development.

The system enabled rapid postwar recovery and growth — the 'Golden Age' of capitalism (1945-1973), with high growth, low unemployment, low inequality.

The system collapsed when Nixon ended dollar-gold convertibility in 1971. Floating exchange rates have prevailed since.

concepts.title: Cold War Economies
concepts.contentHtml:
Two competing economic systems: capitalism (mostly West) vs. central planning (USSR and allies). Both were industrial; both grew rapidly initially; both promised to provide for citizens better than the other.

By the 1970s-80s, Soviet economies were stagnating, lacking innovation, and burdened by military spending. The 1989-1991 collapse of communism and the dissolution of the USSR ended this contest.

China's 1978 reforms began a different path — market reforms within Communist Party rule. By 2010, China was the world's second-largest economy.

concepts.title: Neoliberal Globalization
concepts.contentHtml:
From the late 1970s, deregulation, financial liberalization, and free trade became dominant policies. Reagan, Thatcher, and the Washington Consensus promoted the model. Trade barriers fell; capital flowed across borders.

Global trade reached all-time highs. Hundreds of millions in China and elsewhere lifted from poverty. But inequality within rich countries grew; manufacturing job loss, financial crises (1997 Asian, 2008 global), and political backlash followed.

The 2010s-20s saw populist resistance to globalization (Brexit, Trump's tariffs, China's increased state direction). The post-2020 world is partially deglobalizing.

concepts.title: Digital Transformation
concepts.contentHtml:
The internet, smartphones, cloud computing, and AI have transformed economies. New industries (search, social media, e-commerce, streaming, fintech) emerged. Traditional sectors (retail, media, banking) restructured.

Network effects favor a few dominant players: Google, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Meta in the West; Tencent, Alibaba, ByteDance in China. Combined market caps rival small countries' GDPs.

Productivity gains haven't translated into broad wage growth in many developed countries — sparking the 'Solow paradox' debate ('You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics' — Robert Solow).

concepts.title: Inequality
concepts.contentHtml:
Within-country inequality has risen sharply since 1980 in most developed countries. The top 1% share of US income has roughly doubled. Thomas Piketty's Capital in the Twenty-First Century (2013) documented r > g — when return on capital exceeds growth rate, inequality grows.

Between-country inequality has decreased, particularly as China and India grow. Global inequality has fallen on some measures, risen on others.

Inequality of wealth is even greater than of income. Billionaire wealth has grown enormously even when middle-class wealth stagnated.

concepts.title: Climate Economics
concepts.contentHtml:
Climate change is a defining 21st-century economic challenge. Stern Review (2006) estimated costs of inaction at 5-20% of global GDP; cost of mitigation 1-2%. Most economists agree mitigation is the cheaper path.

Carbon pricing (taxes, cap-and-trade) is the most economically efficient policy tool. EU's emissions trading system is the largest existing market. Many other countries have implemented or are considering carbon pricing.

The energy transition is creating new industries (solar, wind, batteries, EVs) and disrupting old ones (coal, oil). Geographic winners and losers will reshape geopolitics over coming decades.
